texts.sub: Psalm 22 in the Greek and Latin Bibles
texts.note: The Greek is the Septuagint, the Koine Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made before the time of Jesus. The Latin is the Vulgate’s Gallican psalter, translated from that Greek, so the two match closely. English translations written for this site, one for each.
enG: The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.
In a place of green grass, there he has made me dwell; beside water of rest he has nourished me.
He has restored my soul. He has led me on paths of righteousness, for his name's sake.
For even if I walk in the middle of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because you are with me; your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.
You have prepared a table before me, facing those who afflict me; you have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, which makes me drunk, is the very best.
And your mercy will pursue me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.
enL: The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing.
In a place of pasture, there he has set me. Beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up;
he has turned back my soul. He has led me on the paths of justice, for his name's sake.
For even if I walk in the middle of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.
You have prepared a table in my sight against those who trouble me; you have anointed my head with oil, and my cup, which makes me drunk, how splendid it is!
And your mercy will follow me all the days of my life, so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.

texts.note: Greek prose of the early centuries AD (the collection edited by Chambry): plain and close to Koine, but not New Testament Greek. English translations written for this site.

items.en: The good things were driven out by the bad things, because they were weak, and they went up to heaven. The good things asked Zeus how they should live among people. He told them not to go to people all together, but one at a time. That is why bad things come to people constantly, since they live close by, while good things come more slowly, coming down from heaven. So no one quickly finds good things, but everyone is struck by bad things day after day.

An eagle and a fox made friends and decided to live near each other, so that living close would make their friendship firm. So the eagle flew up into a very tall tree and built a nest there, and the fox went into the thicket below and had her cubs. Once, when the fox had gone out to look for food, the eagle, short of food, swooped down into the thicket, snatched up the cubs, and feasted on them with its own chicks. When the fox came back and learned what had happened, she was grieved not so much by the death of her young as by the thought of revenge: as an animal of the land, she could not chase a bird. So she stood far off and cursed her enemy, which is all that is left to the powerless and the weak. But before long the eagle paid the penalty for betraying their friendship. Some people were sacrificing a goat in the country, and the eagle swooped down and carried off a burning piece of meat from the altar. When it reached the nest, a strong wind blew up and lit a bright flame from the thin, old twigs. The chicks were burned and fell to the ground, for they were still too young to fly, and the fox ran up and ate them all in front of the eagle. The fable shows that those who betray a friendship, even if they escape punishment from those they have wronged because they are weak, still cannot escape punishment from God.

items.t: The Eagle and the Dung Beetle
items.en: An eagle was chasing a hare. The hare had no one to help him, but seeing a dung beetle, the only help that chance offered, he begged him for protection. The beetle encouraged him, and when he saw the eagle coming near, he begged it not to carry off the one who had come to him for help. But the eagle, scorning how small he was, devoured the hare before the beetle's eyes. From then on the beetle bore a grudge. He kept watch on the eagle's nests, and whenever the eagle laid eggs, he flew up high, rolled the eggs out and smashed them. At last the eagle, driven out everywhere, fled to Zeus (the bird is sacred to that god) and begged him to give it a safe place to raise its young. Zeus let it lay its eggs in his own lap. When the beetle saw this, he made a ball of dung, flew up, and when he was over Zeus's lap he dropped it there. Zeus wanted to shake the dung off, and as he stood up he threw out the eggs without noticing. Since then, they say, eagles do not nest in the season when dung beetles appear. The fable teaches us to despise no one, remembering that no one is so weak that, when insulted, he cannot one day take revenge.

items.t: The Eagle, the Jackdaw and the Shepherd
items.en: An eagle swooped down from a high rock and snatched a lamb. A jackdaw saw this and, out of envy, wanted to copy it. So it dropped with a great whoosh onto a ram. But its claws got tangled in the wool, and it flapped about, unable to rise, until the shepherd, noticing what had happened, ran up and caught it. He clipped its wing feathers, and when evening came he took it home to his children. When they asked what kind of bird it was, he said: “As far as I know for certain, a jackdaw; but as it would like to think, an eagle.” So rivalry with those who are greater not only achieves nothing but earns laughter on top of misfortune.

items.t: The Eagle with Clipped Wings and the Fox
items.en: An eagle was once caught by a man, who at once plucked its wing feathers and left it in his house with the hens. The eagle was downcast with grief. But another man bought it and soon let its feathers grow again. The eagle flew off, caught a hare, and straight away brought it as a gift to the man who had helped it. A fox saw this and called out: “Don't give gifts to this man; give them to the first, in case he catches you again and strips you of your feathers once more.” The fable shows that we should repay those who help us, but keep clear of the wicked.

items.t: The Eagle Shot with an Arrow
items.en: An eagle was sitting high on a rock, looking to hunt hares. Someone shot it with an arrow. The arrow went into it, and the end of the shaft with its feathers stood before the eagle's eyes. Seeing it, the eagle said: “This is a second grief for me, to die by my own feathers.” The sting of grief is sharper when danger comes from one's own.

A nightingale was sitting on a tall oak, singing as usual. A hawk saw her and, since it had nothing to eat, swooped down and caught her. About to be killed, she begged it to let her go, saying that she was not enough to fill a hawk's belly; if it needed food, it should go after bigger birds. The hawk answered: “I would be mad if I let go of the food ready in my claws to chase what is not even in sight.” So too among people, those are foolish who, hoping for greater things, let go of what they have in hand.

There were many mice in a certain house. A cat learned of this, went there, and caught and ate them one by one. The mice, being picked off all the time, slipped down into their holes, and the cat, no longer able to reach them, decided it must lure them out by a trick. So it climbed up a peg, hung itself from it, and pretended to be dead. But one of the mice peeped out, saw it, and said: “My friend, even if you turn into a sack, I won't come near you.” The fable shows that sensible people, once they have learned how wicked someone is, are no longer fooled by their pretending.

Two roosters were fighting over the hens, and one drove the other away. The beaten one went off and hid in a shady place, while the winner flew up, stood on a high wall and crowed at the top of his voice. At once an eagle swooped down and carried him off. And the one hidden in the dark had the hens to himself from then on, without fear. The fable shows that the Lord opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.

items.t: The Fisherman Who Played the Pipes
items.en: A fisherman who was skilled at playing the pipes took his pipes and his nets and went down to the sea. Standing on a jutting rock, he first made music, thinking the fish would leap out to him of their own accord at the sweet sound. But when, though he kept at it a long time, nothing came of it, he put down his pipes, took up his casting net, threw it into the water and caught many fish. As he tipped them out of the net onto the shore and saw them flapping about, he said: “You worst of creatures! When I was playing, you would not dance, but now that I have stopped, you do.” The fable suits those who do things at the wrong time.

items.t: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
items.en: A fisherman let down his net and brought up a little fish. It begged him to let it go for now, since it was small, and to catch it later, when it had grown, for a bigger profit. The fisherman said: “I would be very foolish to let go of the gain in my hand to chase an uncertain hope.” The fable shows that a gain in the present, even if it is small, is better than one you hope for, even if it is large.

items.t: The Fisherman Who Beat the Water
items.en: A fisherman was fishing in a river. He stretched out his nets so that they closed off the current from bank to bank, tied a stone to a cord, and beat the water with it, so that the fish would flee and fall unawares into the meshes. One of the people who lived nearby saw him doing this and complained that he was muddying the river and not letting them drink clear water. He answered: “But if the river is not stirred up like this, I shall have to starve to death.” So too the demagogues in cities do best when they have driven their countries into civil strife.

The kingfisher is a bird that loves to be alone and always lives on the sea. It is said that, to keep safe from people who hunt it, it builds its nest on rocks by the sea. Once, when she was about to lay her eggs, she came to a headland, saw a rock above the sea, and made her nest there. One day, when she had gone out to feed, the sea, whipped up by a violent wind, rose as high as the nest, flooded it, and drowned the chicks. When the kingfisher came back and saw what had happened, she said: “How wretched I am! I guarded against the land as a danger and fled to the sea, which has proved far more treacherous to me.” So too some people, while guarding against their enemies, fall without knowing it among friends far worse than their enemies.

items.t: The Fox with a Swollen Belly
items.en: A hungry fox saw some bread and meat that shepherds had left in the hollow of an oak. She crept in and ate it all. But her belly swelled up so that she could not get out, and she groaned and wailed. Another fox passing by heard her groaning, came up and asked what was wrong. When she learned what had happened, she said: “Well, stay there until you are as thin as you were when you went in, and then you will get out easily.” The fable shows that time solves difficulties.

A hungry fox saw bunches of grapes hanging from a vine that climbed a tree. She wanted to get them, but could not. As she went away, she said to herself: “They're not ripe.” So too some people, unable to manage things because they are too weak, blame the circumstances.

A fox got into a flock of sheep, picked up one of the suckling lambs and pretended to cuddle it. When a dog asked her what she was doing, she said: “I'm nursing it and playing with it.” The dog said: “Well, if you don't let go of that lamb, I'll give you the dog treatment.” The fable suits a rogue and a foolish thief.

items.t: The Fox and the Monkey Who Was Made King
items.en: At a meeting of the animals, the monkey danced, won great praise, and was elected king. The fox was jealous of him. She had seen a piece of meat lying in a trap, so she led him there and told him she had found a treasure but had not used it herself; she had kept it for him as a privilege of his kingship, and she urged him to take it. He went up to it carelessly and was caught in the trap. When he accused the fox of luring him into it, she said: “Monkey, with so little sense, you rule over the animals?” So those who rush into things without thinking end up laughed at as well as unlucky.

A fox fell into a well and had to stay there. A goat, overcome by thirst, came to the same well and, seeing her, asked whether the water was good. She was delighted at her luck and praised the water at great length, saying it was excellent, and urged him to come down. Thinking only of his thirst, he climbed down without a second thought, and once he had drunk his fill, he began to look with the fox for a way up. The fox said: “I know a good plan, if only you are willing to save us both. Plant your front feet against the wall and hold your horns up straight; I will run up and pull you up after me.” He readily agreed, and the fox leapt up by way of his legs, his shoulders and his horns, reached the mouth of the well, climbed out and went off. When the goat blamed her for breaking their agreement, she turned and said to him: “My friend, if you had as much sense as you have hairs in your beard, you would not have gone down before you had worked out how to get up.” So sensible people should first consider how things will end, and only then set about them.

items.t: The Fox Who Lost Her Tail
items.en: A fox had her tail cut off in a trap. Thinking her life not worth living for shame, she decided she must bring the other foxes to the same state, so as to hide her own defect in a misfortune they all shared. So she gathered them all together and urged them to cut off their tails, saying that a tail was not only ugly but an extra weight hanging from them. One of them answered: “My dear, if this were not to your own advantage, you would not be advising it to us.” This fable suits those who give advice to their neighbours not out of goodwill but for their own advantage.

items.t: The Fox Who Had Never Seen a Lion
items.en: A fox who had never seen a lion met one by chance. The first time she saw him, she was so frightened that she nearly died. When she met him a second time, she was afraid, but not as much as before. The third time she saw him, she grew so bold that she went up and chatted with him. The fable shows that getting used to things makes even frightening things less fearsome.

A fox got into a sculptor's workshop and was searching through everything in it. When she came upon a tragic actor's mask, she lifted it up and said: “What a head, and it has no brain!” The fable suits a man who is impressive in body but foolish in mind.

A pentathlete who was always being taunted by his fellow citizens for his lack of courage went abroad. When he came back some time later, he boasted that he had done many brave deeds in other cities, and that in Rhodes he had made such a long jump that no Olympic champion could match it. He said he would bring as witnesses the people who had been there, if they ever came to town. One of the bystanders answered: “My friend, if this is true, you need no witnesses. Here is Rhodes, and here is the jump!” The fable shows that where something can be proved by deeds, all talk is unnecessary.

A rich Athenian was sailing with some other people. A violent storm arose and the ship capsized. All the others began to swim, but the Athenian kept calling on Athena and promising her endless offerings if he were saved. One of his fellow castaways, swimming past, said to him: “Call on Athena, but move your arms too!” So we too, while we call on the gods, must also think for ourselves and act. It is better to win the favour of the gods while working than to hope to be saved by heaven while doing nothing for ourselves. Those who fall into misfortune must work hard for themselves too, and only so ask God for help.

texts.sub: The prologue and 30 fables in Latin verse
texts.note: Phaedrus, a freed slave of the emperor Augustus, retold Aesop’s fables in Latin verse in the first century AD. English translations written for this site.

items.en: Aesop is the author who found this material; I have polished it in six-beat verses. This little book has a double gift: it makes you laugh, and it gives you wise advice for living. But if anyone wants to complain that trees talk, not just animals, let him remember that we are joking in made-up stories.

A wolf and a lamb had come to the same stream, driven by thirst. The wolf stood upstream and the lamb far below. Then the robber, urged on by his greedy jaws, picked a quarrel. “Why,” he said, “have you muddied the water I am drinking?” The woolly one answered, trembling: “Please, how can I do what you complain of, wolf? The water runs down from you to where I drink.” Beaten back by the force of the truth, the wolf said: “Six months ago you spoke ill of me.” The lamb answered: “But I was not even born.” “Then, by Hercules, your father spoke ill of me,” said the wolf, and so he seized him and tore him apart, an unjust death. This fable is written for those people who crush the innocent with made-up charges.

items.t: The Frogs Ask for a King
items.en: When Athens flourished under fair laws, wild freedom threw the city into confusion and licence broke its old restraint. Then, as the factions plotted, the tyrant Pisistratus seized the citadel. When the Athenians wept over their grim slavery (not because he was cruel, but because any burden is heavy to those wholly unused to it) and began to complain, Aesop told them this little fable. The frogs, roaming their free marshes, asked Jupiter with a great clamour for a king, who would restrain their loose ways by force. The father of the gods laughed and gave them a little log, which, thrown in suddenly, frightened the timid race with the splash and the noise. When it had lain sunk in the mud for some time, one frog happened to put her head quietly out of the pond, inspected the king, and called all the others out. Putting aside their fear, they swam up eagerly, and the cheeky crowd jumped up onto the wood. When they had covered it with every kind of insult, they sent to Jupiter asking for another king, since the one they had been given was useless. Then he sent them a water snake, which began to seize them one by one with its sharp teeth. Helpless, they tried in vain to escape death; fear choked their voices. So they secretly gave Mercury a message for Jupiter, asking him to help them in their distress. Then the god answered: “Since you would not put up with your good king, put up with a bad one.” “You too, citizens,” said Aesop, “bear with this one, so that a worse one does not come.”

items.t: The Proud Jackdaw and the Peacock
items.en: So that no one should want to boast of what belongs to others, but rather live in his own clothes, Aesop has given us this example. A jackdaw, swollen with empty pride, picked up some feathers that had fallen from a peacock and dressed himself in them. Then, despising his own kind, he joined the beautiful flock of peacocks. They tore the feathers off the shameless bird and drove him away with their beaks. Badly beaten, the jackdaw sadly started back to his own kind, but they drove him off too, and he suffered a bitter disgrace. Then one of those he had once looked down on said: “If you had been content with our home and willing to accept what nature gave you, you would not have suffered that insult, and you would not now be feeling this rejection in your misfortune.”

items.t: The Dog Carrying Meat across a River
items.en: Whoever reaches for what belongs to another rightly loses his own. A dog carrying a piece of meat was swimming across a river when he saw his own reflection in the mirror of the water. Thinking it was another dog carrying another prize, he tried to snatch it. But his greed was fooled: he let go of the food he held in his mouth, and could not even reach what he was after.

items.t: The Cow, the Goat, the Sheep and the Lion
items.en: A partnership with the powerful can never be trusted; this little fable proves my point. A cow, a she-goat and a sheep, patient under wrongs, were partners with a lion in the woods. When they had caught a huge stag, the lion divided it into parts and said: “I take the first part because my name is Lion; the second you will give me because I am strong; then, because I am mightier, the third will follow me; and anyone who touches the fourth will be sorry.” So wickedness alone carried off the whole prize.

Aesop saw the lavish wedding of a neighbour who was a thief, and at once began to tell this story: Once, when the Sun wanted to take a wife, the frogs raised a clamour to the stars. Disturbed by the uproar, Jupiter asked why they were complaining. Then one of the pond-dwellers said: “As it is, one Sun burns up all the pools and makes us poor things die in a dried-up home. What will happen if he has children?”

items.t: The Fox and the Tragic Mask
items.en: A fox happened to see a tragic actor's mask. “What a fine face,” she said, “but it has no brain!” This is said of those to whom Fortune has given honour and glory, but taken away common sense.

Whoever wants a reward from the wicked for his services does wrong twice: first, because he helps the unworthy, and second, because he cannot get away unharmed. When a bone a wolf had swallowed stuck in his throat, he was overcome by great pain and began to tempt the animals one by one with a reward to pull the thing out. At last a crane was persuaded by his oath and, trusting the length of her neck to his throat, performed a dangerous operation on the wolf. When she asked for the reward they had agreed on, he said: “You are ungrateful: you have taken your head out of my mouth unharmed, and you ask for payment?”

items.t: The Sparrow Gives the Hare Advice
items.en: That it is foolish to give advice to others and not look out for yourself, we will show in a few lines. A sparrow was scolding a hare that had been seized by an eagle and was weeping bitterly: “Where is that famous speed of yours?” he said. “Why did your feet stop like that?” While he was speaking, a hawk caught the sparrow himself off guard and killed him as he cried out in useless complaint. The hare, half dead, said, as a comfort in death: “You, who a moment ago mocked our troubles without a care, now weep over your own fate with the same complaint.”

items.t: The Wolf and the Fox, with the Monkey as Judge
items.en: Whoever has once become known for shameful deceit is not believed even when he tells the truth. A short fable of Aesop proves it. A wolf accused a fox of theft; she denied that she was anywhere near guilty. Then a monkey sat as judge between them. When each had finished pleading, the monkey is said to have given this verdict: “You, wolf, do not seem to have lost what you claim; you, fox, I believe, stole what you so prettily deny.”

items.t: The Ass and the Lion Go Hunting
items.en: A man with no courage who boasts in words fools strangers but is a joke to those who know him. A lion, wanting to go hunting with a little ass as his companion, hid him in the bushes and told him to frighten the animals with his strange voice, while he himself caught them as they fled. Long-ears suddenly raised a cry with all his strength and threw the beasts into confusion with this new wonder. As they rushed in terror for the paths they knew, they were struck down by the lion's dreadful attack. When the lion was tired of killing, he called the ass out and told him to stop braying. Then the ass said boldly: “What do you think of the work my voice did?” “Outstanding,” said the lion, “so much so that, if I had not known your character and your kind, I would have run away in fear too.”

This story shows that things you have despised often turn out more useful than things you have praised. A stag, after drinking at a spring, stood still and saw his reflection in the water. As he admired and praised his branching antlers and found fault with his legs for being too thin, he was suddenly frightened by the shouts of hunters and began to run across the plain, and with his light running he escaped the dogs. Then a wood took in the wild creature; there his antlers were caught and held, and he began to be torn apart by the savage bites of the dogs. Dying, he is said to have spoken these words: “Unhappy me! Only now do I understand how useful the things I despised were to me, and how much grief the things I praised have brought.”

Whoever enjoys being praised with crafty words usually pays for it with shameful regret. A crow, perched high in a tree, wanted to eat a piece of cheese he had snatched from a window. A fox saw him and began to speak like this: “Oh, crow, how your feathers shine! How much beauty there is in your body and your face! If you had a voice, no bird would be finer.” But the foolish crow, trying to show off his voice, let the cheese fall from his mouth, and the cunning fox quickly snatched it up with greedy teeth. Only then did the deceived crow groan at his own stupidity. This shows how much cleverness is worth: wisdom always wins out over strength.

A bad cobbler, ruined by poverty, began to practise medicine in a place where no one knew him and to sell an antidote under a false name, and with wordy tricks he won himself a reputation. When the king of the city lay worn out by a serious illness, he called for a cup to test him. Then he poured in water, pretended to mix poison into the man's antidote, and ordered him to drink it himself, offering a reward. Then, for fear of death, the man confessed that he had become a famous doctor not through any skill in medicine but through the stupidity of the crowd. The king called an assembly and added: “How mad do you think you are, when you do not hesitate to trust your heads to a man to whom nobody would give his feet to be shod?” I would say this truly applies to those whose foolishness makes a profit for the shameless.

items.t: The Ass and the Old Shepherd
items.en: When a country changes its rulers, the poor usually change nothing but the character of their master. This little fable shows it is true. A timid old man was grazing his little ass in a meadow. Suddenly frightened by the shouting of the enemy, he urged the ass to run away so that they would not be captured. But the ass, in no hurry, said: “Tell me, do you think the conqueror will put two packsaddles on me?” The old man said no. “Then what does it matter to me whom I serve, as long as I carry my own packsaddle?”

items.t: The Sheep, the Stag and the Wolf
items.en: When a cheat calls on dishonest men to guarantee a loan, he does not want to settle the matter but to cause harm. A stag asked a sheep to lend him a measure of wheat, with the wolf as his guarantor. But she, suspecting a trick, said: “The wolf is always in the habit of snatching and running off, and you of vanishing from sight at full speed. Where shall I look for you when the day comes?”

items.t: The Sheep, the Dog and the Wolf
items.en: Liars usually pay the penalty for their misdeeds. A dog, making a false claim, demanded from a sheep a loaf of bread he said he had lent her. The wolf, called as a witness, said that not just one loaf was owed, but ten. The sheep, condemned on false testimony, paid what she did not owe. A few days later the sheep saw the wolf lying in a pit. “This,” she said, “is how the gods above reward deceit.”

No one gladly goes back to the place that hurt him. A woman whose months were complete and whose child was about to be born lay on the ground, weeping and groaning. Her husband urged her to lie down on the bed, where she could better lay down nature's burden. “Not at all,” she said. “I have no faith that the trouble can end in the same place where it began.”

A bad man's flattery hides a trap; the lines below warn us to avoid it. A dog who was about to give birth asked another dog to let her have her puppies in her kennel, and easily got her way. Then, when the owner asked for her place back, she pleaded with her, begging for a little time, until she could lead out her puppies when they were stronger. When this time too had run out, the owner began to demand her bed more forcefully. “If you can match me and my pack,” said the dog, “I will give up the place.”

A foolish plan not only fails but also leads mortals to ruin. Some dogs saw a hide sunk in a river. To get it out and eat it more easily, they began to drink up the water; but they burst and died before they could reach what they were after.

items.t: The Old Lion, the Boar, the Bull and the Ass
items.en: Whoever has lost his former standing becomes a joke even to cowards in his misfortune. A lion, worn out by age and abandoned by his strength, lay drawing his last breath, when a boar came up to him with flashing tusks and avenged an old wrong with a blow. Soon a bull gored his enemy's body with hostile horns. The ass, seeing that the wild beast could be hurt without punishment, kicked in his forehead with his hooves. But the lion, dying, said: “It was hard to bear the brave insulting me; but having to bear you, disgrace of nature, I feel I am dying twice.”

A weasel, caught by a man and wanting to escape the death that threatened her, said: “Please spare me, for I clear your house of troublesome mice.” The man answered: “If you did it for my sake, it would be welcome, and I would have pardoned you as you ask. But since you work to enjoy the scraps the mice would have gnawed, and to eat the mice themselves as well, don't charge me for a favour that is no favour.” And with these words he put the wicked creature to death. Those people should recognise that this is said about them, who serve their own private interest and boast to the unwary of their empty services.

A man who is suddenly generous pleases fools, but sets useless traps for the wise. When a thief at night had thrown a dog some bread, testing whether he could be won over by the food he offered, the dog said: “Hey, do you want to tie my tongue, so that I won't bark to protect my master's property? You are badly mistaken. This sudden kindness of yours tells me to stay awake, so that you do not profit through any fault of mine.”

items.t: The Frog Who Burst and the Ox
items.en: A poor man who tries to copy the powerful comes to ruin. Once, in a meadow, a frog saw an ox and, touched with envy at its great size, puffed up her wrinkled skin. Then she asked her children whether she was bigger than the ox. They said no. Again she stretched her skin with a greater effort and asked in the same way which of them was bigger. They said the ox. At last, indignant, as she tried to puff herself up even harder, she burst and lay dead.

Those who give bad advice to cautious people both waste their effort and are shamefully laughed at. It is said that dogs drink from the river Nile while running, so as not to be seized by crocodiles. So when a dog had begun to drink while running, a crocodile said: “Lap as much as you like, at your leisure; don't be afraid.” But the dog said: “By Hercules, I would, if I did not know how hungry you are for my flesh.”

No one should be harmed; but if anyone does harm, this fable warns that he should be paid back in kind. A fox, they say, was the first to invite a stork to dinner, and set before her a thin soup on a flat dish, which the hungry stork could not taste at all. When the stork invited the fox in return, she set out a narrow-necked jar full of minced food. Putting her beak into it, she ate her fill herself, and tortured her guest with hunger. As the fox licked the neck of the jar in vain, we are told the travelling bird spoke like this: “Everyone should calmly put up with being treated the way he treats others.”

items.t: The Dog, the Treasure and the Vulture
items.en: This story may suit misers, and those who, born poor, want to be called rich. A dog digging up human bones found a treasure; and because he had offended the gods of the dead, he was filled with a greed for riches, so that he would pay the penalty to holy religion. And so, while he guarded the gold and forgot about food, he wasted away from hunger. A vulture standing over him is said to have spoken: “Dog, you lie there as you deserve, for you suddenly longed for a king's wealth, though you were conceived at a crossroads and brought up on a dunghill.”

However high up they are, the mighty should fear the lowly, because revenge lies open to a ready wit. Once an eagle carried off a fox's cubs and put them in her nest for her chicks to feed on. The mother followed her and began to beg her not to bring such grief on her, poor creature. The eagle scorned her, since she was safe up in that place. The fox snatched a burning torch from an altar and surrounded the whole tree with flames, threatening her enemy with grief and the loss of her young. To rescue her own from the danger of death, the eagle humbly handed the cubs back to the fox unharmed.

items.t: The Frogs Afraid of the Bulls' Battle
items.en: The lowly suffer when the powerful quarrel. A frog in a marsh, watching a fight between bulls, said: “Oh, what destruction is coming for us!” Asked by another frog why she said this, since the bulls were fighting over the leadership of the herd and lived far away from them, she said: “Their home is apart and their kind is different; but the one who is driven from his rule over the woods and runs away will come to the hidden hiding-places of the marsh and crush us under his hard hooves. So their fury reaches our heads.”

Whoever puts himself in the care of a wicked man finds ruin while he looks for help. When the doves had often fled from the kite and escaped death by the speed of their wings, the robber turned his mind to deceit and tricked the defenceless race with this ruse: “Why do you live in fear, rather than make a treaty with me and make me your king, to keep you safe from every harm?” Believing him, they handed themselves over to the kite; and once he had gained the throne, he began to eat them one by one and to rule with cruel claws. Then one of those who were left said: “We are punished as we deserve.”
